chunks.content: Key Points Introduction Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a hemodynamic condition defined, according to the 6th world Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) as mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) above 20 mmHg at rest [ , ]. PH is a progressive disease, causing severe symptoms with a poor prognosis leading to right sided heart failure (RHF) in group 2 PH, which is the majority of patients with PH undergoing mitral valve repair surgery. The prevalence of PH in general is agreed to be higher in young patients, particularly females. However, the prevalence among patients above 65 years is also likely to occur owing to other underlying comorbidities, such as left heart disease. On the other hand, USA and Europe data supports the high prevalence among the elderly even in case of arterial PH [ , ]. PH can be primary or secondary. Secondary causes of PH include, but not limited to, underlying pathology (such as pulmonary and left sided cardiac disease), drugs, toxins, or certain infections [ , ]. Clinically, PH can be classified into five groups based on the pathophysiology: group 1, caused by pulmonary artery disease, which could be idiopathic or hereditary; group 2, caused by left sided heart disease e.g., left sided heart failure; group 3, caused by pulmonary disease and/or hypoxia; group 4, caused by pulmonary artery obstruction e.g., chronic thromboembolism; and finally group 5, which can be caused by multifactorial mechanisms. Group 2 and 3 PH are frequently found in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. In patients with group 1 PH, hemodynamics are characterized by an elevated mPAP above 20 mmHg, with a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) ≤ 15 mmHg, reflecting isolated pulmonary vascular pathology. Conversely, in group 2 PH, which is linked to left heart disease including mitral valve disease, patients demonstrate both elevated mPAP and PCWP > 15 mmHg, indicative of pulmonary venous hypertension resulting from left-sided heart dysfunction. In mixed pre- and post-capillary PH, seen in some patients with advanced heart disease, both mPAP and PCWP are elevated, often accompanied by increased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), highlighting the complex interplay between pulmonary vascular and left-sided heart dysfunction [ – ]. Regardless of the etiology, patients with PH express the same pathologic changes, including prolonged vasoconstriction and pulmonary vascular remodeling, which eventually lead to increased pulmonary vascular resistance, subsequently elevating the right ventricular pressure [ , ]. Pre-existing PH prior to cardiac surgery poses a significantly increased risk of morbidity and mortality which can be aggravated by multiple factors, including extracorporeal circulation, mechanical ventilation, and the use of general anesthesia [ – ]. Multiple mechanisms are attributed to right ventricular (RV) failure including: the elevated afterload resulting from the maladaptation to the increased vascular resistance, the poor contractile reserve of the right ventricle, and the arrest during the surgical procedure [ ]. Therefore, optimization of the perioperative cardiopulmonary pressures is paramount to avoid unnecessary adverse events such as acute right-sided heart failure and delayed extubating. Currently, available medical therapies for group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension target mostly one of three essential pathways: prostacyclin, endothelin (ET), and nitric oxide (NO) causing smooth muscle relaxation and pulmonary vasodilation with subsequent reduction in the pulmonary artery pressure [ ]. However, they are harmful in some cases of pulmonary venous hypertension as they can provoke pulmonary edema if in a patient with mitral valve disease [ ]. Thus, careful perioperative optimization of PH in patients undergoing cardiac surgery can be challenging with lack of existing knowledge in this area. The aim of this network meta-analysis is to compare the efficacy of various pulmonary vasodilators in perioperative optimization of PH in those patients with the goal of addressing the existing knowledge gap. Methods This network meta-analysis was carried out on the basis of a predetermined protocol registered in Open Science Framework with registration link https://doi.org/ 10.17605/OSF.IO/7HMJ2, and was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension statement for network meta-analysis (NMA PRISMA 2020) [ , ]. Search Strategy and Data Collection We conducted a comprehensive and systematic literature search of five electronic databases, including PubMed, Cochrane Central Registry of Controlled Trials, Scopus, Embase and Web of Science (WOS) from inception to 17 September 2024. The search strategy has been formulated based on the key terms of previous studies. These keywords were the interventions, the condition of interest and the type of surgery. The search Strategy was: (“mitral valve surgery” OR “valve surgery”) AND “Pulmonary hypertension” AND (“sildenafil” OR “levosimendan” OR “milrinone” OR “nitroglycerin” OR “dexmedetomidine” OR “iloprost” OR “nitric oxide” OR “dobutamine” OR “Sodium nitroprusside” OR “Prostacycline” OR “Enoximone”). We included only randomized-controlled trials (RCTs) involving vasodilator intervention and its impact on hemodynamics of pulmonary hypertension patients undergoing mitral valve surgery compared with another vasodilator or placebo group. The search Strategy was: (“mitral valve surgery” OR “valve surgery”) AND “Pulmonary hypertension” AND (“sildenafil” OR “levosimendan” OR “milrinone” OR “nitroglycerin” OR “dexmedetomidine” OR “iloprost” OR “nitric oxide” OR “dobutamine” OR “Sodium nitroprusside” OR “Prostacycline” OR “Enoximone”). We included only randomized-controlled trials (RCTs) involving vasodilator intervention and its impact on hemodynamics of pulmonary hypertension patients undergoing mitral valve surgery compared with another vasodilator or placebo group. We also searched the reference lists of the relevant RCTs to add any missing RCT from our preliminary search and clinicaltrials.gov to look for unpublished or ongoing studies. All RCTs were included with no language or publication period limitations. Selection Criteria We included studies that met the following requirements: (1) population: this review considered all studies that involved patients of any age and sex undergoing mitral valve surgery, and had pulmonary hypertension diagnosed using the gold standard right heart catheterization method or echocardiography. The cutoff values of diagnosing PH in the included studies were MPAP ≥ 25 mmHg or SPAP ≥ 35 mmHg. Studies that included combined interventions in one arm compared with placebo or control group in the other arm were excluded. (2) Interventions: studies where the experimental (or exposed) group received sildenafil, levosimendan, milrinone, nitroglycerin, dexmedetomidine, iloprost, nitric oxide, or dobutamine treatment; (3) comparators: studies where the control group received sildenafil, levosimendan, milrinone, nitroglycerin, dexmedetomidine, iloprost, nitric oxide, dobutamine, or placebo (patients who were not exposed to vasodilators therapy prior to or during the valve surgery); (4) outcomes: comparing the efficacy of different vasodilators in managing perioperative pulmonary hypertension. The efficacy was determined on the basis of the hemodynamic changes from perioperative period to the last available follow-up period in each study. The hemodynamic variables include heart rate (HR), mean arterial pressure (MAP), mean pulmonary arterial pressure (MPAP), pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), cardiac output (CO), cardiac index (C.I), central venous pressure (CVP), systolic pulmonary artery pressure (SPAP), and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP). All outcomes were continuous and expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and number of patients. (5) Study design: we included only randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Study Screening and Data Extraction Four reviewers independently screened the articles’ titles and abstracts based on the eligibility criteria of inclusion. Reviewers were blinded by each other's decisions. After exclusion of non-eligible studies, the remaining studies underwent full text screening by the same method. Conflicts were resolved through reviewers’ discussion with the assistance of the first review author to determine the final decision. The screening process was done using Rayyan software [ ]. We extracted the relevant data into three electronic sheets: (1) summary sheet: contains the basic information of each study, which are study design, country, number of centers, total participants, follow-up duration, main inclusion criteria, primary outcomes, and conclusion; (2) baseline sheet: contains the baseline characteristics of patients in each study. Baseline characteristics include age, sex, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and body mass index (BMI). The categorical data were shown as event frequency and its percentage whereas the continuous data were shown as mean and standard deviation. We extracted the mean and SD for the intervention group and the comparative group separately. For studies not measuring BMI and containing weight and height, we calculated BMI utilizing this equation: BMI (kg/m 2 ) = weight (Kg)/ height (m 2 ). (3) outcome sheet: this sheet is for the hemodynamics changes. Our outcomes of interest were heart rate (HR), mean arterial pressure (MAP), mean pulmonary arterial pressure (MPAP), pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), cardiac output (CO), cardiac index (C.I), central venous pressure (CVP), systolic pulmonary artery pressure (SPAP), and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP). We extracted outcome values at baseline and at the end of follow- up. All outcomes were expressed as mean ± SD. Not all studies contain all the prespecified outcomes, we considered these missing data in data cleaning and manipulation. For studies that report data in graphical format only, we used Web plot digitizer version to extract these data. Quality Assessment We used the Revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (ROB 2.0) [ ] to assess the quality of the eligible RCTs. It includes five domains of bias: randomization process, deviations from the intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. Five reviewers independently reviewed the included studies. Studies were classified based on each domain separately into low risk, some concerns or high risk. Each domain’s final decision was taken based on significant questions answered with “yes,” “probably yes,” “probably no,” “no,” or “no information” according to algorithms suggested by ROB 2.0. Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (ROB 2.0) [ ] to assess the quality of the eligible RCTs. It includes five domains of bias: randomization process, deviations from the intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. Five reviewers independently reviewed the included studies. Studies were classified based on each domain separately into low risk, some concerns or high risk. Each domain’s final decision was taken based on significant questions answered with “yes,” “probably yes,” “probably no,” “no,” or “no information” according to algorithms suggested by ROB 2.0. Any disagreements were resolved by discussion or with the assistance of the first review author. Statistical Analysis To carry out this network meta-analysis (NMA), we utilized the netmeta package accessible through RStudio. The data was aggregated as mean difference (MD) for continuous outcomes and risk ratio (RR) for dichotomous outcomes, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) provided for each outcome. We assessed and measured substantial heterogeneity using the Chi-squared (Q2) and I squared tests, respectively. Forest plots were generated for each predefined outcome. We identified significant heterogeneity as a Breslow–Day test I 2 > 50% or a P value < 0.1. In the presence of significant heterogeneity, the random effect model was employed. The results of our NMA, including all estimated values, were presented in a league table for ease of comparison. Results Study Selection After removing duplicate entries, the initial electronic database searches yielded 377 unique records. Through the process of titles and abstracts screening, 285 were excluded. A total of 92 records for full text screening. Among these, 73 records were excluded owing to inappropriate study design, population, intervention, or lack of relevant outcomes. Among the remaining 19 studies [ – , – ], 2 studies compared [ , ] different routes for the same treatment, which are not relevant for the other study that does not mention the route of each drug or our network (Fig. ) Study Characteristics The objective of this clinical research paper was to assess the efficacy of different pulmonary vasodilators in patients undergoing mitral valve surgery. 17 studies [ , , – ] involving 862 patients were analyzed to investigate the impact of these vasodilators. The studies utilized various measurements to evaluate the outcomes. Those measurements were divided into three categories: pulmonary measures, systemic measures, and cardiac measures. In terms of pulmonary measures, four specific parameters were examined, mean pulmonary arterial pressure (MPAP), systolic pulmonary arterial pressure (SPAP), pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCW). While systemic measures included three parameters, central venous pressure (CVP), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), and mean arterial pressure (MAP). Cardiac measures included three parameters as well, cardiac output (CO), cardiac index (C.I), and heart rate (HR). The study examined ten unique treatment options, which were categorized into three groups. Group 1 included nitric oxide (NO), sodium nitroprusside, and nitroglycerin. Group 2 included phosphodiesterase inhibitors, such as enoximone and milrinone. Lastly, group 3 included prostacyclin analogues (prostacyclin and iloprost). The detailed summary and baseline characteristics for the included studies are presented in Tables and , respectively. Quality Assessment After applying The Cochrane Risk of Bias (ROB 2) tool to evaluate the quality of the included studies, most of the included studies showed low risk of bias in most of the domains. Ersoy 2013, Fattouch 2005, and Fattoucha 2006 [ , , ] showed high risk of bias owing to randomization, while Fattouch 2005 and Mishra 2016 [ , ] showed high risk of bias owing to missing data. Jiang 2013 and Eskandr 2018 [ , ] showed high risk of bias as well owing to selection of reported results. The rest of the studies showed low risk of overall bias. The risk of bias summary and graph are shown in Figs. and , respectively. Network Meta-Analysis Results We included 17 studies in the analysis. All the included studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that examined the effects of different vasodilators. The studies focused on three pulmonary measures, namely MPAP, SPAP, and PCWP, with 22, 8, and 15 pairwise comparisons, respectively. Systemic measures, including MAP and SVR, had 19 and 14 pairwise comparisons, while cardiac measures, such as HR and CI, had 13 and 19 pairwise comparisons. Although additional outcomes, such as PVR, CVP, and CO, were considered, no network meta-analyses (NMAs) could be performed owing to a lack of connectivity between treatments. Fixed-effects models were employed for all the measure except for MPAP, for which random-effects models were found to be more suitable for these two measures. Pulmonary Measures Our analysis shows that none of the treatments showed significant efficacy compared to placebo in reducing PCWP and SPAP (Figs. , ). However, for MPAP, prostacyclin, nitric oxide (NO), and sodium nitroprusside demonstrated statistically significant reduction in MPAP when compared with placebo [MD, 95% CI: (− 11.77, − 18.78; − 4.76; − 8.3–15.9,−0.61; and − 11.02, − 20.1; − 3.8, respectively] (Fig. ). The heterogeneity was significant for MPAP and PCWP, ( I 2 = 61.6%, 26%, 80.1% and I 2 = 75%, 43.4%, 89%, respectively) indicating variability among the studies, while SPAP showed low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 22.7%, 0%, 73.4%). To address the heterogeneity and inconsistency, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by excluding the studies that contributed large heterogeneity and inconsistency for MAPAP and PCWP measures. Study 5 and 6 [ ] was excluded for MPAP, while studies 4 and 17 [ , ] were excluded for PCWP. The revised models showed improvements in model fit. Sildenafil showed a statistically significant reduction in MPAP (MD, 95% CI: (− 2.9, − 5.5; − 0.29), while both NO and sildenafil showed a statistically significant reduction in PCWP (MD, 95% CI: −6.64, −12.48; −0.80; 4.80, 0.90; 8.7) respectively. The heterogeneity in the revised models was reduced compared with the initial models ( I 2 = 46.1%,0%, 75% and I 2 = 28.3%, 0%, 73.4%). The observed heterogeneity for MPAP and PCWP was found to be specific to certain treatment comparisons rather than common across all comparisons. After conducting sensitivity analyses and excluding studies contributing to large heterogeneity (study 5 and 6 for MPAP and studies 4 and 17 for PCWP), the heterogeneity was reduced, indicating that the variability was driven primarily by these specific comparisons rather than being a generalized issue across all comparisons. We applied the SUCRA scores to rank the treatments based on their efficacy. Sildenafil (79%), nitric oxide(78%), and milrinone (89%) were ranked higher for decreasing MPAP, PCWP, and SPAP, respectively. Systemic Measures The analysis revealed that NO, prostacyclin, and sodium nitroprusside showed significant reductions in MAP, with effect sizes (MD, 95% CI: 24, 15; 33; 18.9, 10; 27.8; 22.6, 10; 27.8 , respectively) (Fig. ). Additionally, NO, prostacyclin, sodium nitroprusside, and nitroglycerin demonstrated significant reductions in systemic vascular resistance (SVR), with effect sizes of (MD, 95% CI: − 0.54, − 0.82; − 0.26; − 0.37, − 0.65; − 0.09; − 0.47, − 0.77; − 0.16; − 0.14, − 0.24; − 0.03, respectively) (Fig. ). The heterogeneity observed in the two models was low, with I 2 values of 0%. This indicates that there was a minimal variability among the studies included in the analysis. Furthermore, there was no evidence of inconsistency in either model, as indicated by the non-significant Q values ( I 2 = 0%, 0% ,67.6%; I 2 = 0%, 0%, 84.7%). Enoxamine was found to be the most effective in reducing MAP, with a SUCRA score of 81%. In contrast, NO had the lowest SUCRA score of 6%, suggesting it was the least effective in reducing MAP. For SVR, levosimendan had the highest positive impact with a SUCRA score of 91%, while sildenafil was the least likely to have a positive impact on SVR, with a SUCRA score of 12%. Cardiac Measures The analysis showed that none of the treatments had a significant effect on heart rate (HR) (Fig. ). However, several treatment options, including iloprost, levosimendan, milrinone, nitroglycerin, nitric oxide (NO), and prostacyclin, showed significant increases in cardiac index (C.I). Subgroup Analysis Regarding subgrouping, we split patients into those with heart failure and those without. For patients with heart failure, we looked at MPAP, PCWP, C.I, and HR using NMA. For patients without heart failure, we only considered SPAP. We could not perform NMA for the resting measure owing to a lack of connection between the designs. Patients with Heart Failure In patients with heart failure, NO showed a significant decrease in MPAP from the baseline (MD, 95% CI: 13.73, − 23.7; − 3.8 ), with a highest SUCRA score of 71%. I 2 for heterogeneity/inconsistency = 59.1% (0%, 84.7%) (Supp Fig.1). For PCWP, sildenafil exhibited a significant increase (MD, 95% CI: 4.8, 2.4; 7.3). NO ranked highest in terms of SUCRA score by 80% and a I 2 for heterogeneity/inconsistency = 48.1% (0%, 84.8%) (Supp Fig.2). In terms of cardiac index, sildenafil achieved the highest score of 96%, while levosimendan achieved the highest score for heart rate at 69%. I 2 for heterogeneity / inconsistency = 24.2% (0%, 92.1%) and 7% (0%, 90.3%), respectively (Supp Figs. 3 and 4). Patients Without Heart Failure Sildenafil shows significant reduction from the baseline for SPAP (MD, 95% CI: − 6.5, 12.3; − 0.83) and ranked highest in terms of SUCRA score at 86%. I 2 for heterogeneity/inconsistency = 0% (0%, 7%) (Supp Fig.5). Discussion Preoperative PH is a known risk factor for increased morbidity and mortality after mitral valve surgery [ ]. In this current network meta-analysis, the investigators compared the effect of various vasodilators in perioperative management of PH during mitral valve surgery. The primary findings showed the following: (I) prostacyclin, NO, and sodium nitroprusside demonstrated a significant reduction in MPAP; (II) none of the vasodilators showed significant efficacy in reducing PCWP or SPAP; (III) NO, prostacyclin, and sodium nitroprusside exhibited a significant reduction in MAP and SVR; (IV) enoximone showed the most reduction in MAP; (V) levosimendan had the highest positive impact on SVR; (VI) iloprost, levosimendan, milrinone, nitroglycerin, NO, and prostacyclin showed a significant increase in the cardiac index (C.I), and the highest positive impact was with milrinone and levosimendan; (VII) none of the treatment options had a significant effect on HR; and (VIII) in patients with heart failure, NO significantly reduced MPAP, while sildenafil increased pressure PCWP and achieved the highest C.I. In patients without heart failure, sildenafil significantly reduced SPAP. The findings of our NMA offer a comprehensive understanding of the impact on cardiac performance. In a study by Patel et al., showed that several pulmonary vasodilators can be used in PH including inhaled prostacyclin and NO to reduce PAPs, PVR, and improve cardiac output in patients with pulmonary hypertension resulting from MVD after surgery. Though short‐term use of these pulmonary vasodilators in the postoperative period appears safe [ ]. Another study by Sardo et al., showed that inhaled prostacyclin was the only vasodilator whose use is supported by a statistically discernible improvement in mortality in the perioperative cardiac surgery setting as treatment of pulmonary hypertension [ ]. The clinical implications of these hemodynamic improvements, particularly their potential to translate into better postoperative outcomes, such as decreased morbidity, mortality, and long-term survival, need further clarification. While previous studies have demonstrated the efficacy of reducing MPAP and improving C.I in the perioperative period [ , ], the mechanisms through which these improvements lead to better clinical outcomes, such as reduced right ventricular failure [ ], improved long-term cardiac function, and survival rates [ ], remain underexplored. For instance, PHTN is strongly associated with increased mortality and heart failure readmissions after mitral valve repair [ ], and postoperative hemodynamic factors, such as increased PAP and PVR, have been linked to worse outcomes, including right heart failure and mortality [ ]. The improvement in MPAP and C.I does suggest a beneficial effect, but long-term follow-up studies and more detailed investigations into patient-centered outcomes are necessary to confirm whether these hemodynamic changes translate into improved postoperative

For instance, PHTN is strongly associated with increased mortality and heart failure readmissions after mitral valve repair [ ], and postoperative hemodynamic factors, such as increased PAP and PVR, have been linked to worse outcomes, including right heart failure and mortality [ ]. The improvement in MPAP and C.I does suggest a beneficial effect, but long-term follow-up studies and more detailed investigations into patient-centered outcomes are necessary to confirm whether these hemodynamic changes translate into improved postoperative recovery and survival [ , ]. Moreover, although our study highlights the effectiveness of vasodilators in managing perioperative pulmonary hypertension [ ], the literature lacks comprehensive evaluations of how these interventions impact long-term survival, quality of life, and the risk of complications, such as right-sided heart failure, arrhythmias, and prolonged ICU stay post-surgery [ ]. In a study on severe heart failure patients undergoing mitral valve repair, elevated biomarkers such as high-sensitive troponin T and low mixed venous oxygen saturation were predictive of worse prognosis, including increased mortality [ ]. Therefore, future studies should aim to bridge this gap by conducting longitudinal analyses that focus on these outcomes in the context of mitral valve surgery and heart failure management. Efforts to improve earlier intervention, before the onset of severe PHTN, may further enhance patient outcomes [ ]. Our analysis emphasized the challenge of managing PH during mitral valve surgery, where the patients face elevated risks of complications and mortality. The study aimed to provide more clarity in the selection of vasodilator agents, addressing the scarcity of solid evidence and the current reliance on individual judgment and existing meta-analyses. Strengths The study utilized a rigorous systematic review and meta-analysis approach following PRISMA guidelines. The inclusion of a network meta-analysis allowed for a comprehensive comparison of multiple vasodilators, providing a nuanced understanding of their efficacy. The sensitivity analysis addressed heterogeneity and inconsistency and enhanced the robustness of the findings. Limitations The study limitations include the presence of high risk of bias in some included studies. Additionally, heterogeneity and inconsistency were observed in certain outcomes, leading to the exclusion of specific studies in the sensitivity analysis. Finally, the lack of relationship between treatments with some outcomes restricted the conduct of network meta-analyses. Not all the medications discussed, such as milrinone, are specific pulmonary vasodilators. While milrinone primarily functions as an inotrope for heart failure, its inclusion in our analysis was on the basis of its vasodilatory effects and role in overall hemodynamic optimization. This broad approach to medication selection may limit the direct applicability of our findings to pulmonary hypertension management alone. Future studies could benefit from focusing more narrowly on interventions specifically targeting pulmonary hypertension to refine therapeutic strategies. Lastly, the data were not sufficient to conduct a reliable subgroup analysis based on the heart failure status of the patients in all the outcomes. Recommendations for Future Studies Future studies should focus on conducting well-designed randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with low risk of bias to strengthen the evidence base. Addressing the limitations observed in this analysis, such as heterogeneity and inconsistency, will contribute to more reliable and generalizable findings. Further studies are warranted to explore the long-term outcomes and adverse effects of vasodilator in the context of PH during cardiac surgery. Conclusions In summary, our NMA highlights prostacyclin, NO, and sodium nitroprusside as consistently effective in reducing MPAP during mitral valve surgery in the setting of PH. These medications exhibit positive impacts on systemic parameters, lowering MAP and SVR. Milrinone and levosimendan emerge as valuable choices, enhancing C.I without significantly affecting HR. These findings offer insights for clinicians, suggesting prostacyclin, NO, sodium nitroprusside, milrinone, and levosimendan as promising options for perioperative optimization of hemodynamics in patients with PH prior to mitral valve surgery. While acknowledging study limitations, these results contribute to refining treatment strategies and call for future well-designed trials to explore long-term outcomes and adverse effects associated with these interventions.
